# Thermochemistry — 2.2 Specific Heat and Calorimetry

<!-- ExamScribe draft. Chapter ch02, section part 2.2, pages 8–10. Source: chapters/ch02/source/2.2.md -->

::: concept T-heat-capacity
term: Heat capacity
definition: [p.8: "The heat capacity (C) of an object is the amount of heat needed to raise its temperature by 1 °C."]
plain: Heat capacity is about a whole object: it depends on both what the object is made of and how much of it there is. [p.8: "Heat capacity depends on both the kind of substance and its amount."]
misconception: Wrong: heat capacity and specific heat capacity mean the same thing. | Right: specific heat capacity is for 1 gram of a substance and does not depend on the amount. [p.8: "Specific heat is an intensive property: it depends only on the kind of substance, not on the amount."]
:::

::: concept T-specific-heat-capacity
term: Specific heat capacity
definition: [p.8: "The specific heat capacity (c) of a substance is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 gram of the substance by 1 °C."]
plain: Specific heat capacity is the heat needed per gram, so it depends only on the kind of substance, not on how much of it there is. [p.8: "Specific heat is an intensive property: it depends only on the kind of substance, not on the amount."]
example: Water's specific heat is 4.184 J/(g·°C), much higher than copper's 0.385 J/(g·°C). [p.9: "water (liquid) 4.184 aluminum 0.897 iron 0.449 copper 0.385"]
ai-mnemonic: "Specific" means "per gram": c is small letter, small amount (1 g); C is capital, the whole object.
:::

::: formula EQ-2.1
name: Heat for a temperature change
latex: q = m \times c \times \Delta T
where: q = heat (J); m = mass (g); c = specific heat (J/(g·°C)); ΔT = final minus initial temperature (°C). [p.8: "where q is the heat in joules, m is the mass in grams, c is the specific heat in J/(g·°C), and ΔT is the change in temperature (final temperature minus initial temperature)."]
holds-when: Only when the sample changes temperature without changing phase. [p.8: "The heat absorbed or released by a sample that changes temperature without changing phase is given by"]
source: [p.8: "The heat absorbed or released by a sample that changes temperature without changing phase is given by"]
check: q = m * c * dT
rearrange: dT = q / (m * c)
rearrange: c = q / (m * dT)
rearrange: m = q / (c * dT)
example: A positive q means the sample absorbs heat; a negative q means it releases heat. [p.8: "When q is positive the sample absorbs heat; when q is negative the sample releases heat."]
:::

::: worked-example WE-2.1
title: Heat Absorbed by Water
source: Example 2.1 [p.9: "How much heat is absorbed when 250. g of water is heated from 20.0 °C to 35.0 °C?"]
problem: Find the heat absorbed when 250. g of water warms from 20.0 °C to 35.0 °C. [p.9: "How much heat is absorbed when 250. g of water is heated from 20.0 °C to 35.0 °C?"]
step: Find the temperature change, final minus initial: 35.0 °C − 20.0 °C = 15.0 °C.
step: Use q = m × c × ΔT with c = 4.184 J/(g·°C) for water (Table 2.1).
step: Multiply: 250. g × 4.184 J/(g·°C) × 15.0 °C = 15,690 J, which is 15.7 kJ.
step: q is positive, so the water absorbed heat.
calc: dT = 35.0[degC] - 20.0[degC] => 15.0[degC]
calc: q = 250[g] * 4.184[J/(g*degC)] * dT => 15690[J]
calc: q => 15.7[kJ]
result: q = 15,690 J = 15.7 kJ, absorbed by the water. [p.9: "= 15,690 J = 15.7 kJ. Because q is positive, the water absorbed heat."]
:::

::: concept T-calorimeter
term: Calorimeter
definition: [p.9: "A calorimeter is a device used to measure the heat that flows during a chemical or physical process."]
plain: In a coffee-cup calorimeter a reaction happens in water inside an insulated cup, and the water's temperature change gives the heat. [p.9: "In a simple coffee-cup calorimeter, a reaction takes place in water inside an insulated cup, and the temperature change of the water is used to calculate the heat released or absorbed by the reaction."]
why: Because the cup is insulated, the heat released by the reaction is taken to equal the heat absorbed by the water. [p.10: "Because the calorimeter is insulated, we assume that the heat released by the reaction equals the heat absorbed by the water"]
figure: FIG-2.2
:::

::: figure TAB-2.1
what: Table 2.1 lists specific heats at 25 °C: water 4.184, aluminum 0.897, iron 0.449 and copper 0.385 J/(g·°C). [p.9: "Table 2.1 Specific Heats of Common Substances at 25 °C"] [p.9: "water (liquid) 4.184 aluminum 0.897 iron 0.449 copper 0.385"]
look-for: Water has by far the highest specific heat in the table. [p.9: "water (liquid) 4.184 aluminum 0.897 iron 0.449 copper 0.385"]
:::

::: figure FIG-2.2
what: A coffee-cup calorimeter: nested foam cups keep heat from leaking to the surroundings. [p.10: "A coffee-cup calorimeter. Nested foam cups limit heat exchange with the surroundings."]
:::

::: question Q-2.2-01
type: mcq
bloom: understand
ask: Why is specific heat capacity called an intensive property?
option A: It depends only on the kind of substance, not on the amount.
option B: It depends on both the kind of substance and its amount.
option C: It can be measured only for water.
option D: It is the heat needed to warm a whole object by one degree.
answer: A
why: The book calls specific heat intensive because it depends only on the kind of substance. [p.8: "Specific heat is an intensive property: it depends only on the kind of substance, not on the amount."]
why-not B: That describes heat capacity, which also depends on the amount. [p.8: "Heat capacity depends on both the kind of substance and its amount."]
why-not C: Table 2.1 gives specific heats for several substances, not only water. [p.9: "water (liquid) 4.184 aluminum 0.897 iron 0.449 copper 0.385"]
why-not D: That is heat capacity, which is defined for a whole object. [p.8: "The heat capacity (C) of an object is the amount of heat needed to raise its temperature"]
covers: LO-2.2-1, T-specific-heat-capacity, T-heat-capacity
:::

::: question Q-2.2-02
type: numeric
bloom: apply
ask: How much heat is needed to warm 50.0 g of aluminum from 25.0 °C to 75.0 °C? Use c = 0.897 J/(g·°C).
calc: dT = 75.0[degC] - 25.0[degC] => 50.0[degC]
calc: q = 50.0[g] * 0.897[J/(g*degC)] * dT => 2242.5[J]
answer: 2.24[kJ]
why: Use q = m × c × ΔT, with ΔT taken as final minus initial temperature. [p.8: "ΔT is the change in temperature (final temperature minus initial temperature)"]
covers: LO-2.2-2, EQ-2.1
:::

::: question Q-2.2-03
type: cloze
bloom: remember
ask: A ____ is a device used to measure the heat that flows during a chemical or physical process.
answer: calorimeter
why: The device that measures the heat flowing in a chemical or physical process is called a calorimeter. [p.9: "A calorimeter is a device used to measure the heat that flows during a chemical or physical process."]
covers: LO-2.2-3, T-calorimeter
:::

::: question Q-2.2-04
type: tf
bloom: understand
ask: If q is negative for a sample, the sample released heat.
answer: true
why: A negative q means the sample releases heat. [p.8: "when q is negative the sample releases heat"]
covers: LO-2.2-2, EQ-2.1
:::
